purpose: Ungraded, problem-first Android/Fire OS challenges. A topic is a navigational aid, not a mandatory prerequisite. Challenges may be approached at any abstraction level: scripting through native code and OS diagnostics; lower does not imply deeper.

challenges.title: Why does a remote press sometimes trigger two actions?
challenges.problem: Observe actual KeyEvents and UI actions on Fire OS. Find when one physical gesture becomes multiple application actions, and design a minimally invasive interpretation that remains predictable.
tacit_checks: Capture a reproducible raw-versus-accepted input trace
Explain one duplicate-action failure using observed events
Change one normalization rule and compare the real result
possibility_seeds: Could a normalized intent-event stream make different remote and game-controller hardware interchangeable?
What would change if the interface showed a visible virtual pointer rather than relying on focus alone?

challenges.title: What happens when Android interrupts an unfinished task?
challenges.problem: Build a tiny stateful interaction; switch to Home, force recreation and, when practical, process loss. Determine which state survives, which does not, and why.
tacit_checks: Distinguish view recreation from process death
Restore a visible in-progress state after recreation
Document one intentionally unrecoverable case
challenges.local_start: Create a small independent app; never clear existing Console/browser data.
possibility_seeds: Could every game and experiment resume after a crash without saving full process memory?
What is the smallest state an agent would need to reconstruct a lost interactive session?

challenges.title: Can a game change its animation without rebuilding its engine?
challenges.problem: Load a tiny versioned external sprite bundle, then alter it independently of the game. Compare updates, cache reuse, version rollback and offline behavior.
tacit_checks: Update an asset independently of engine code
Show an unchanged cached asset is reused
Reopen with the previous verified asset when offline
challenges.local_start: Start with the native Playroom microgames as a rendering/control baseline; external loading remains unimplemented.
possibility_seeds: Could an animation artist change the TV experience by updating only a versioned asset project?
What if one animation pack could be shared across several games without sharing game logic?

challenges.title: Can an iPad make a complex TV interface genuinely usable?
challenges.problem: Compare remote-only interaction with an optional iPad companion for a pointer/keyboard-intensive application. Observe latency, focus, reconnect and permission boundaries.
tacit_checks: Measure an end-to-end input round trip
Recover gracefully after losing connection
Distinguish app-local input from system-wide injection
challenges.local_start: Treat TV-first control as the baseline; no background companion service exists yet.
possibility_seeds: Which interactions become practical when the iPad handles text and precise input while TV owns the display?
Could one semantic command work equally through touch, remote, voice and agent?

challenges.title: Why can ten lines of animation code stutter?
challenges.problem: Draw a simple moving sprite using JavaScript/Canvas or a tiny native Android View. Change one factor at a time; explain whether visible jitter comes from the animation clock, input delivery, the renderer, or the device's display pipeline.
tacit_checks: Measure frame intervals rather than guessing by eye
Compare a scripted and Android-view implementation with the same motion
Identify a device-dependent bottleneck without blaming the language prematurely
partial_progress_examples: Found one measurable source of jank
challenges.local_start: Fire Browser HTML input lab and Playroom's native 2D games are starting references; scripted frame diagnostics are a new exercise, not yet a built-in instrument.
possibility_seeds: What if a game transmitted intended motion as data rather than streaming every rendered frame?
Could a deliberately jittery animation teach us the limits of remote control latency?

challenges.title: Can a tiny C function be slower than Java?
challenges.problem: Implement the same bounded transformation in Java and Android NDK C/C++. Compare not only raw arithmetic but also the cost and correctness of crossing JNI, native allocations, and transferring arrays.
tacit_checks: Package an NDK library for the actual device ABI
Measure repeated calls and batched calls fairly
Explain why fewer JNI crossings can outperform a seemingly faster native function
challenges.local_start: Use a standalone Android NDK sample or independent test module; Fire Console does not currently bundle an NDK demo.
possibility_seeds: Could keeping a small state machine native avoid expensive cross-language calls?
When might a native module become portable between games and other kinds of Android experiments?

challenges.title: What can an app and ADB actually know about Android?
challenges.problem: Compare information visible inside a normal app with information returned by a separately authorized ADB session. Identify where app sandboxing, shell privileges and protected system services impose real boundaries.
tacit_checks: Collect a narrow, non-sensitive app-local diagnostic report
Use supported ADB diagnostics to observe a system service
Identify an unavailable operation and explain its permission boundary without trying to bypass it
challenges.local_start: The existing Fire test helper and Input Lab are relevant. Authorized ADB is optional and not a prerequisite to other Dojo projects.
possibility_seeds: Which low-level observations could become a safe user-facing capability browser?
Could exposing a carefully selected system signal help the human invent new game mechanics?

challenges.title: Can a tiny Python script produce a meaningful TV experiment?
challenges.problem: Have an external Python program produce a simple visual or state update for a TV-owned app through a narrow, inspectable content protocol. Identify which parts actually execute remotely versus on Fire OS, and how disconnections affect the intended behavior.
tacit_checks: Make a scripted change visible on the TV without modifying the core engine
Observe a remote failure without losing the last working state
Explain why script length does not predict engineering depth
challenges.local_start: Start with versioned assets and the existing Playroom; dynamic asset streaming or script invocation is not yet implemented.
possibility_seeds: What could an external Python agent generate that the TV can display without compiling a new APK?
Could a TV be the interactive face of many independently updated computational experiments?

challenges.title: Where does a native Android program stop having authority?
challenges.problem: Trace one ordinary app's input, filesystem or graphics operation toward its OS/kernel boundary using public code, permitted device observations and optionally an emulator. Separate the effects of native machine code from privileged kernel operations.
tacit_checks: Identify the relevant ordinary Android/NDK API
Find an observable boundary and explain the expected failure/success
Distinguish behavior on a test emulator from the actual Fire TV
partial_progress_examples: Observed a permitted app-local native call
Identified a driver-level question requiring another environment
challenges.local_start: Research-and-observation challenge only on ordinary Fire TV. Kernel changes belong to a separate authorized simulator or development device.
possibility_seeds: Can we infer a system boundary without crossing it, through behavior and source analysis?
What physical phenomena would an emulator reveal or hide compared with this Fire TV?

stack_levels.label: SCRIPT / WEB / DECLARATIVE
stack_levels.description: JavaScript, HTML Canvas, locally authored web tools, manifests and externally executed Python. Small programs still support rigorous Android experiments if traced to device behavior.
stack_levels.boundary: A remote Python worker is not native Android execution; WebView JavaScript has its own security and lifecycle behavior.

stack_levels.label: ANDROID APPLICATION / FRAMEWORK
stack_levels.description: Java/Kotlin application components, Activities, lifecycle, events, UI widgets, assets, storage, rendering and permissions.
stack_levels.boundary: Ordinary apps receive only their own allowed inputs and resources; a TV app is not a global remapper.

stack_levels.label: NATIVE / ABI / HARDWARE-FACING
stack_levels.description: Android NDK C/C++, JNI, .so libraries, CPU/ABI, memory, native performance, OpenGL ES and supported platform APIs.
stack_levels.boundary: Native code is still inside the Android application sandbox; it does not imply root or kernel privileges.

stack_levels.label: SYSTEM OBSERVATION / ADB
stack_levels.description: With authorized ADB, inspect supported system diagnostics using logcat, dumpsys and process/device instrumentation. Compare application observations with system reports.
stack_levels.boundary: Availability varies by Fire OS build and shell permissions; diagnostic read access is not arbitrary modification authority.

stack_levels.label: KERNEL / FIRMWARE / DRIVERS
stack_levels.description: Understand the kernel boundary, SELinux, driver interfaces, boot architecture and hardware design via sources, emulators or other authorized test devices.
stack_levels.boundary: Do not presume root, bootloader unlock, kernel module loading, firmware replacement, or modification of protected services on ordinary Fire TV.

holistic_purpose: Increase the human's intuition, creativity, and judgment about what the TV might make possible. Experiments, topics and agents serve that capability; finishing exercises is never the goal.
